newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico to keep eye on consumption after GDP surge.
newsitem.headline: Mexico to keep eye on consumption after GDP surge.

text.p: Mexico's Deputy Finance Minister Martin Werner said on Tuesday he would be worried if consumption started to outstrip production and jeopardize efforts to promote domestic savings.

In an interview with Reuters Financial Television a day after the government released second-quarter GDP data that beat even the most bullish forecasts, Werner said he was not concerned that 8.8 percent growth was too rapid.
"The only concern we will have is if consumption grows faster than output," he said in the live television interview, but added, "We dont think now that that will be the case."
Economists are now looking ahead to the release next month of the supply and demand breakdown of the GDP numbers for a better indication of how deep the recovery really is.

Some are concerned that the prospect of a consumer boom would erode policies geared to boosting domestic savings -- considered crucial to protect Mexico against the volatility of foreign capital flows.
"In the middle of September we will release the figures for aggregate demand components for these growth numbers that we've just released," Werner said.
"In case we see consumption growing significantly higher than output, and therefore domestic savings dropping, then we would be concerned," he said.
He said Mexico needed growth but not a consumer boom that would erode efforts to promote domestic savings.
"If we see consumption growing slower than output, then we have the type of scenario that we want," he said, adding it was crucial to see domestic savings increase as the growth process consolidated.
He said the second-quarter GDP numbers underlined how firm the recovery actually was.

"The strength of the data points to the strength of the recovery in the Mexican economy, the fact that the service sector is picking up and also the fact that the agricultural sector is now turning out very positive numbers," he said.
In the same interview, he said Mexico's 1997 GDP growth was likely to exceed the official forecast of 4.5 percent.
"Right now we feel (year-end GDP) is probably higher than 4.5 percent, but we are not yet revising our forecasts," he said. ((--Caroline Brothers, Mexico City newsroom +525 728 7905))
